figures.finding: No collective agreement, union rate card or statutory minimum sets a South African actor's pay in film, television or on the stage: actors are engaged as independent contractors and the fee is whatever the producer offers and the actor accepts; the 2025 competition exemption lets SAGA negotiate only guideline rates, which may not be prescribed.

value.engagement: independent contractor (contract law, not labour law)

figures.applies: South Africa, film, television, commercials and stage, as of 2026-11-01.

sources.said: People in the film and television and the performing arts industries are independent contractors, not employees, and are covered under contract law, and not labour law, in South Africa … “Producers will go to actors and hand them a contract and say: ‘These are the conditions of work. This is the rate. Take it or leave it.’”

Classified as independent contractors, we have been denied the basic worker rights that many take for granted, including the right to form a union and to engage in collective bargaining. … Our efforts to provide guidance on fair compensation through a recommended minimum rate card were challenged by the Competition Commission

Under competition law we could not even discuss issues like standardized contracts, minimum rates and certain employment conditions within the industry. Now with the exemption we can! We can begin to draft contracts and present them to industry to be standardized. We can meet with productions and producers to negotiate minimum rates guidelines.

The Applicants and their members shall commit to using the minimum rate cards as guidelines for starting negotiations with market participants and not prescribe the minimum rate cards to the industry.

figures.finding: The Competition Commission granted SAGA and the Personal Managers Association a conditional five-year exemption (13 December 2024 to 12 December 2029, Government Gazette 52013, Notice 2954 of 31 January 2025) to design guideline rate cards with minimum rates and negotiate standard contracts with producers, on condition the rate cards are used only as starting points for negotiation and never prescribed; the producers' appeal was withdrawn in June 2025, and by 20 February 2026 negotiations were still under way with no agreement or rate card concluded.

value.gazette: Government Gazette No. 52013, General Notice 2954 of 2025

figures.finding: The Minister of Employment and Labour gave notice on 23 January 2026 (Government Gazette No. 53987) of the intention to deem performers employees for parts of the BCEA, the National Minimum Wage Act, COIDA and the LRA; comments closed on 22 February 2026, and no final notice was found by 2026-11-01, so the national minimum wage does not yet reach actors.

value.instrument: Notice of intention under section 83 of the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997

figures.applies: South Africa, performers in advertising, artistic and cultural activities; proposed, not in force.

sources.said: hereby give notice of my intention to deem all performers in the performance of advertising, artistic and cultural activities as employees for the following:
2. The National Minimum Wage Act, 2018 (Act No. 9 of 2018).

The Minister’s notice, published in Government Gazette No. 53987 on 23 January 2026, is a welcome – and long overdue – step in the right direction. It proposes to deem performers in advertising, artistic and cultural activities to be employees for the purposes of specific provisions in key labour statutes … Deem performers in advertising, artistic and cultural activities to be employees for the purposes of specific provisions in the Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA), the National Minimum Wage Act (NMWA), the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA), and parts of the Labour Relations Act (LRA).
Submissions are now closed (since 22 February 2026) … hereby give notice of intention to deem all performers in the performance of advertising, artistic and cultural activities as employee.

figures.finding: The one statutory instrument for performers, Sectoral Determination 10, sets no pay for child performers under 15 but caps their working hours at four a day over age ten and three a day at ten or younger, and their time at the workplace at ten, eight or six hours by age; their pay goes to a parent or guardian.

value.instrument: Sectoral Determination 10: Children in the Performance of Advertising, Artistic and Cultural Activities (Notice No. R. 882 of 2004)

figures.applies: South Africa, children under 15 in advertising, artistic and cultural activities, from 2004 (in force as of 2026-11-01 per SAGA).

sources.said: (a)in respect of a child aged over ten years, four hours a day; … (b)in respect of a child of ten years or younger, three hours a day. … (a)ten hours, in the case of a child aged over ten years; … (b)eight hours, in the case of a child aged older than five years but not older than ten years; … (c)six hours, in the case of a child aged younger than five years.
(1)This Determination applies to the employment of children under 15 years of age in the performance of advertising, artistic and cultural activities.
(1)Any remuneration due to a child must be paid to the parent or legal guardian of the child—

Since 1997, Sectoral Determination 10 has regulated the employment of children in performance, treating them as employees for the purposes of defined provisions of the BCEA and setting out additional safeguards.

figures.finding: The actors' body is the South African Guild of Actors (SAGA), a non-profit company with more than 500 members; Full Membership costs R160 a month by debit order, Associate Membership R850 a year up front (for up to two years), and Student Membership is free; no agreement exists that could make membership a condition of being cast.

value.name: South African Guild of Actors (SAGA)
value.eligibility: any actor legally entitled to work in South Africa, engaged or about to be engaged; may be asked to show training or work experience

figures.applies: South Africa, actors in film, television, stage, commercials and corporate work.

sources.said: SAGA Full Membership is open to any actor legally entitled to work in South Africa. They should be engaged or about to be engaged as an actor in the film, theatre and television industry. Prospective members may be required to demonstrate to the satisfaction of the SAGA Executive Committee that they have the necessary training or work experience to be considered as professionals within the industry. … Full Membership is currently R 160 paid monthly by debit order. … Associate Membership has an annual up-front payment of R 850. … For absolutely zero fees a student can become a Student Member
We cannot negotiate with productions on your behalf, but we can advise you on what clauses mean and what the current trends are.
Saga, which supports actors’ and artists’ rights to fair pay, working conditions and benefits, has more than 500 members.

figures.finding: Television drama is cast mainly in English, with a licensed share in the other official languages: e.tv's licence requires its programming primarily in English and at least 10% of its South African drama in other official languages, and its dramas ran in isiZulu, isiXhosa, Setswana, Sesotho and Afrikaans.

value.rule: e.tv licence: programming primarily in English; at least 10% of South African drama broadcasting time in official languages other than English

figures.applies: South Africa, free-to-air television (e.tv), licence period 17 December 2008 to 16 December 2023, compliance year 2020/21.

sources.said: “Subject to the specific language requirements set out below, the Licensee shall ensure in respect of the licensed service, its programme material is provided primarily in English.” … “At least 10% of the aggregate broadcasting time of its South African drama productions transmitted by the Licensee in a wide range of official languages other than English”. … • “Scandal”, broadcast in isiZulu, Setswana, Sesotho and Afrikaans;

figures.finding: Most filming is in Gauteng (39% of activity), then the Western Cape (25%) and KwaZulu-Natal (12%).
figures.applies: South Africa, film industry, April 2016 to March 2021.

sources.said: According to the respondents, Gauteng (39%), the Western Cape (25%) and KwaZulu-Natal (12%) are the main centres of filming activity, as was the case in the previous study (2016/17).
